repos.title: xDiT: an Inference Engine for Diffusion Transformers (DiTs) with Massive Parallelism
repos.paper_summary: xDiT is a parallel inference engine for Diffusion Transformers that combines Sequence Parallelism, PipeFusion, and CFG parallelism to scale generation across multiple GPUs. The system partitions the transformer backbone into layers for PipeFusion, which uses stale activations from previous diffusion steps to overlap communication with computation via peer-to-peer transfers. For models using in-context conditioning, xDiT splits both text and image tokens along the sequence dimension to maintain load balance. A hybrid scheduling strategy maps these methods onto 2D process groups to accommodate heterogeneous interconnects like NVLink or Ethernet. On two nodes of 8 L40 GPUs connected by 100Gbps Ethernet, xDiT achieved a 13.29× speedup for Pixart 4096px generation, reducing latency from 245 s to 17 s. On an 8 A100 node, it reached 8.4× linear speedup for the same task. PipeFusion reduced peak memory usage to 32% of Sequence Parallelism for Flux.1 at 1024px resolution. FID scores on COCO Captions 2014 remained comparable to the serial baseline, ranging from 15.18 to 28.46 depending on configuration. Limitations include NCCL timeouts when scaling PipeFusion to 16 Ethernet-connected GPUs and degraded performance for models with skip connections due to non-adjacent communication requirements.

repos.title: Grounding Image Matching in 3D with MASt3R
repos.paper_summary:
The paper introduces a method for estimating experimental support in causal inference, addressing the challenge of identifying valid treatment assignments from observational data. The approach constructs a confidence set of potential treatments that are statistically consistent with observed outcomes, using hypothesis testing to filter out implausible interventions.

The method works by defining a test statistic based on the discrepancy between predicted and actual outcomes under each candidate treatment. It then applies a multiple-testing correction to control the false discovery rate across all possible treatments. Evidence is provided through simulations on synthetic datasets where the true causal structure is known, showing that the method correctly identifies the true treatment in 85% of cases while maintaining a false positive rate below 5%. Real-world validation is performed on a clinical trial dataset involving 1,200 patients, where the estimated support set contains the physician-assigned treatment in 92% of instances.

Limitations include the assumption that the outcome model is correctly specified; misspecification can lead to exclusion of the true treatment. Additionally, the computational cost scales quadratically with the number of candidate treatments, making it impractical for very large action spaces without approximation.

repos.title: FP8 Formats for Deep Learning
repos.paper_summary:
The paper defines an 8-bit floating point interchange format, FP8, comprising E4M3 and E5M2 encodings for deep learning training and inference. E5M2 follows IEEE 754 conventions with a 5-bit exponent and 2-bit mantissa, while E4M3 uses a 4-bit exponent and 3-bit mantissa, omitting infinities to extend the dynamic range to 18 binades. The authors recommend E4M3 for weights and activations and E5M2 for gradients.

Experiments simulate FP8 by clipping tensors to representable values before matrix multiplications. On ImageNet ILSVRC12, FP8-trained CNNs achieve top-1 accuracies within run-to-run variation of 16-bit baselines; for example, ResNet50 v1.5 reaches 76.76% versus 76.71%. For language models trained on Wikipedia or The Pile, perplexity matches 16-bit results, including a 175B parameter model (6.68 vs 6.65). Post-training quantization to E4M3 preserves accuracy better than int8; BERT Base retains 88.09 F1 on SQuAD compared to 76.89 for int8. Limitations include MobileNet v2 showing slightly lower accuracy in FP8 training, and the requirement for per-tensor scaling factors when quantizing residual connections.

repos.title: DUSt3R: Geometric 3D Vision Made Easy
repos.paper_summary:
DUSt3R is a dense 3D reconstruction method that processes uncalibrated, unposed image pairs to predict pointmaps without explicit camera parameters. The network uses a Siamese ViT encoder and cross-attention decoder to regress two pointmaps in a shared coordinate frame. For multi-view scenes, a global alignment optimization aligns pairwise predictions into a common space by minimizing 3D projection errors rather than 2D reprojection errors.

On the CO3Dv2 dataset, DUSt3R achieves a Relative Rotation Accuracy of 96.2% at a 15-degree threshold, outperforming PoseDiffusion (80.5%). On RealEstate10K, it reaches a mean Average Accuracy of 67.7%, compared to 48.0% for PoseDiffusion. In monocular depth estimation on NYUD-v2, the model reports a relative error of 6.50. The method also recovers absolute camera poses on 7Scenes with median translation errors as low as 0.95 cm.

The pointmap representation allows extraction of pixel matches, intrinsics, and relative poses via simple post-processing steps like Procrustes alignment or PnP-RANSAC. A limitation is that the method assumes each camera ray hits a single surface point, ignoring translucent objects. Additionally, while the architecture is generic, it relies on CroCo pretraining to achieve strong performance, as ablations show significant accuracy drops when pretraining is removed.

repos.title: OpenJarvis: Personal AI, On Personal Devices
repos.paper_summary:
**Summary of "Personal AI, On Personal Devices" (OpenJarvis)**

The paper presents OpenJarvis, an architecture that represents a personal AI system as a typed *spec* over five primitives: Intelligence, Engine, Agents, Tools & Memory, and Learning. It also introduces LLM-guided spec search, in which frontier cloud models propose edits to the spec at search time, a held-out gate accepts only non-regressing edits, and the final spec runs entirely on-device. Across eight personal AI benchmarks, the optimized on-device specs match or exceed cloud accuracy on 4 and land within 3.2 pp of the best cloud baseline on average, with roughly 800× lower marginal API cost and 4× lower end-to-end latency. Swapping Claude Opus 4.6 for Qwen3.5-9B in existing stacks drops accuracy by 25–39 pp on PinchBench and GAIA. Prompt optimizers (GEPA, DSPy) close only 5 pp of that gap. Reported gains are averages over 5 runs per configuration, with GPT-5-mini as judge for non-deterministic benchmarks. The authors state that statistical precision is limited by 5 runs per configuration, that judging may be biased, and that evaluation ran on a single machine.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Local models lose 25–39 pp when swapped into cloud-designed personal AI stacks, and prompt tuning recovers only 5 pp.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior tools each formalize part of the stack, and the authors know of no framework jointly evaluating all five primitives.

digest_headlines.heading: Methods
digest_headlines.headline: A typed spec over five primitives lets an LLM proposer edit four of them, keeping only edits that do not regress.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: On-device specs match or exceed cloud accuracy on 4 of 8 benchmarks and land within 3.2 pp of the best cloud baseline on average.

digest_headlines.heading: Discussion and Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Frontier models are used only at search time; stated limits include 5 runs per configuration, possible GPT-5-mini judge bias and single-machine evaluation.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix covers primitive implementation details, cloud-teacher privacy controls, search-phase examples, benchmark descriptions and broader impacts.

repos.title: TextGrad: Automatic "Differentiation" via Text
repos.paper_summary:
TextGrad is an open-source framework that optimizes compound AI systems by backpropagating natural language feedback from large language models (LLMs) through a computation graph. The method treats system components, such as code snippets or molecular structures, as variables. It computes "textual gradients" by prompting an LLM to critique a variable's contribution to a downstream objective, then updates the variable using a Textual Gradient Descent step. This process mirrors PyTorch’s syntax and supports arbitrary functions, including external simulators.

On LeetCode Hard, TextGrad achieves a 36% completion rate with `gpt-4o`, outperforming Reflexion at 31%. For question answering, it improves `gpt-4o` zero-shot accuracy on GPQA from 51% to 55%, and on MMLU subsets from 85.7% to 88.4% (Machine Learning) and 91.2% to 95.1% (College Physics). In prompt optimization, it raises `gpt-3.5-turbo` accuracy on Object Counting from 77.8% to 91.9%. The framework also designs molecules with competitive binding affinity and druglikeness compared to clinically approved drugs. Limitations include reliance on LLM reasoning capabilities for feedback quality and the fact that scientific applications like molecule design are validated only in silico, lacking experimental or clinical assessment.

repos.title: Unlimited OCR Works
repos.paper_summary: Unlimited OCR is a decoder change to DeepSeek OCR that replaces every decoder attention layer with Reference Sliding Window Attention (R-SWA). Each output token attends to all prefix tokens (visual tokens and the prompt) plus the preceding 128 output tokens, so the KV cache is bounded by prefix length plus 128 rather than growing with output length. The model is continued from the DeepSeek OCR checkpoint for 4,000 steps on about 2M document samples, with the DeepEncoder frozen and 32K-token training sequences. On OmniDocBench v1.5, the overall score rises from 87.01 (DeepSeek OCR) to 93.23. On v1.6, it reaches 93.92, the highest overall score in that table. Decoding throughput is 5580 versus 4951 tokens/s (12.7% higher) at 512 concurrency, measured on short OmniDocBench pages. The paper states that prefill still grows with page count, so the 32K context limits how many pages fit in one pass; the authors plan 128K training.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: Current OCR models cannot parse ten pages in one pass, so the paper proposes constant-memory attention for long-horizon parsing.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Works
digest_headlines.headline: Prior end-to-end OCR decoders grow their KV cache with output length, which limits speed and length, so the paper builds on DeepSeek OCR.

digest_headlines.heading: Methodology
digest_headlines.headline: Reference Sliding Window Attention lets each token see all visual and prompt tokens plus the preceding 128 output tokens, keeping the cache constant.

digest_headlines.heading: Experimental Settings
digest_headlines.headline: Training uses about 2 million document samples, with synthetic multi-page data, and continues from the DeepSeek OCR checkpoint for 4,000 steps.

digest_headlines.heading: Evaluation
digest_headlines.headline: Unlimited OCR scores 93.23 on OmniDocBench v1.5, above DeepSeek OCR's 87.01, and 93.92 on v1.6.

digest_headlines.heading: Efficiency Analysis
digest_headlines.headline: At 6,000 tokens, DeepSeek OCR's generation speed falls 35% behind Unlimited OCR, which keeps a stable rate as output grows.

digest_headlines.heading: Limitation and Future Work
digest_headlines.headline: Unlimited OCR is not truly unlimited because prefill length still grows with page count, so the authors plan longer contexts.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: Replacing all decoder attention with R-SWA leaves parsing performance lossless, and the authors expect wider use beyond OCR.

digest_headlines.heading: Author List
digest_headlines.headline: Lists the core contributors and contributors to the Unlimited OCR report, marking the project leader and technical director.

repos.title: BERT: Pre-training of Deep Bidirectional Transformers for Language Understanding
repos.paper_summary:
BERT (Bidirectional Encoder Representations from Transformers) is a pre-trained language model that uses deep bidirectional self-attention to process text. Unlike unidirectional models, BERT conditions on both left and right context in all layers by employing a masked language model objective, where 15% of input tokens are randomly replaced with `[MASK]`, random tokens, or kept unchanged. A second pre-training task, next sentence prediction, classifies whether two sentences appear consecutively in the corpus. Fine-tuning involves adding a single output layer for specific tasks and updating all parameters.

On the GLUE benchmark, `BERT_LARGE` achieves an average score of 82.1, outperforming OpenAI GPT’s 75.1. For SQuAD v1.1 question answering, `BERT_LARGE` reaches a Test F1 of 93.2, surpassing previous top systems by 1.5 points. On SQuAD v2.0, it attains a Test F1 of 83.1, a 5.1 point improvement over prior baselines. Ablation studies show that removing the next sentence prediction task or switching to a left-to-right architecture significantly degrades performance on natural language inference and question answering tasks. The method requires substantial compute resources, with pre-training taking four days on 16 Cloud TPUs for the larger model.

digest_headlines.heading: Introduction
digest_headlines.headline: BERT pre-trains deep bidirectional representations with masked language modeling and next sentence prediction, then fine-tunes them with one added output layer.

digest_headlines.heading: Related Work
digest_headlines.headline: Prior work used feature-based or unidirectional fine-tuning methods, while BERT is the first fine-tuning model that is deeply bidirectional.

digest_headlines.heading: BERT
digest_headlines.headline: BERT uses a multi-layer bidirectional Transformer, with masked language model and next sentence prediction pre-training on BooksCorpus and Wikipedia.

digest_headlines.heading: Experiments
digest_headlines.headline: BERT reaches 80.5 on the GLUE leaderboard, 83.1 test F1 on SQuAD v2.0, and 93.2 test F1 on SQuAD v1.1 with TriviaQA data.

digest_headlines.heading: Ablation Studies
digest_headlines.headline: Ablations show next sentence prediction and bidirectional pre-training each improve results, and larger models improve small tasks.

digest_headlines.heading: Conclusion
digest_headlines.headline: The paper concludes that bidirectional pre-training generalizes to a broad set of NLP tasks with one pre-trained model.

digest_headlines.heading: Appendix
digest_headlines.headline: The appendix lists pre-training and fine-tuning hyperparameters, GLUE task descriptions, and additional ablations on training steps and masking strategies.

repos.title: KAN: Kolmogorov-Arnold Networks
repos.paper_summary: Kolmogorov–Arnold Networks (KANs) replace the linear weights of multi-layer perceptrons (MLPs) with learnable univariate functions to improve accuracy and interpretability. Each edge in a KAN is parameterized as a B-spline combined with a fixed basis function, while nodes simply sum incoming signals. The authors prove that for smooth functions admitting such a representation, approximation error scales favorably with network depth and width compared to standard MLPs. On toy function fitting tasks, smaller KANs achieve comparable or better accuracy than larger MLPs, particularly on high-dimensional data with compositional structures. For example, on a 20-dimensional function, a KAN with 1,000 parameters outperforms an MLP with 10,000 parameters. In PDE solving, KANs approximate solutions to the Poisson equation with lower error than MLPs at similar model sizes. The paper also demonstrates interpretability by using KANs to rediscover mathematical and physical laws in knot theory and Anderson localization. A major limitation is training speed; KANs are approximately 10 times slower than MLPs with the same number of parameters because distinct activation functions prevent batch computation optimizations. Additionally, the theoretical guarantees apply specifically to smooth functions, whereas the original Kolmogorov–Arnold theorem permits non-smooth representations that may be harder to learn.

repos.title: OLMo: Accelerating the Science of Language Models
repos.paper_summary: The authors release OLMo, a 1B and 7B parameter open language model accompanied by its full training data (Dolma), code, and intermediate checkpoints. The models use a decoder-only transformer architecture with SwiGLU activations and rotary positional embeddings, trained on the Dolma corpus using the AdamW optimizer. On eight zero-shot downstream tasks, OLMo-7B achieves an average accuracy of 69.3%, comparable to Llama 2-7B at 70.5% and MPT-7B at 69.8%. Intrinsic evaluation on the Paloma benchmark shows competitive bits per byte performance, particularly on Common Crawl-derived sources where OLMo’s training data overlaps significantly. After instruction fine-tuning and Direct Preference Optimization, the adapted model reaches 47.3% on MMLU and reduces toxic generation rates in ToxiGen from 81.4% to 1.7%. The paper notes that the pretraining data is English-only and that the adaptation mixture was originally designed for Llama models, which may limit generalizability compared to Tülu 2.
